meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'верить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to believe', paired with 'верить'.

examples.trans: And everyone believed it?
Believe me.

examples.text: Со своего телефона? И все поверили?
examples.trans: From your own phone? And everyone believed it?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'so, then; like that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
That's good like that.
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be; there is'.

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.
You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'better', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: It's better like this.
I feel better today.
Working. Making people's lives better.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'if', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Come if you want.
And if not?
Take her if you want.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.
And does the governor support you?

examples.text: Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'дохнуть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to drop dead, croak (colloq.)'.

related.gloss: not to to drop dead (negated infinitive)

examples.text: Лучше будет, если вы сдохнете сзади!
examples.trans: It will be better if you drop dead out there!

examples.text: На кухне никто не хочет сдохнуть без причины.
examples.trans: In the kitchen nobody wants to drop dead without a reason.

сзади.gloss: behind, from behind, at the back

meanings.en: behind, from behind, at the back
meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'зади').

examples.trans: Better stay behind me.
Someone is walking behind.
Just stay leaning back.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'otherwise', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Go, or else you'll be late.
I think differently.

examples.text: Пятьдесят метров, не больше. Иначе будет сигнал.
examples.trans: Fifty metres, no more. Otherwise there'll be a signal.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
I'm doing my homework.

выйти.gloss: to go out, to get out

meanings.en: to go out, to get out
meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to go out, to get out', paired with 'выходить'.

examples.text: Я выйду отсюда через две недели.
examples.trans: I'll be out of here in two weeks.
He left the house.

examples.text: Я выйду отсюда через две недели. Я решу все ваши проблемы.
examples.trans: I'll be out of here in two weeks. I'll solve all your problems.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.
Dad and Mum.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'бить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to kill', paired with 'убивать'.

examples.trans: Do you want to kill me?
I'll kill you! (said in anger)

examples.text: Ты смотришь на меня так, как будто убить хочешь.
examples.trans: You look at me as if you want to kill me.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.trans: The chef is in the kitchen.
Chef, I didn't take it.
Cleverly thought out, boss!

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'адекватный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('inappropriate, unhinged').

examples.trans: Chef, you are not in your right mind!

examples.text: Сегодня у шефа очень неадекватный день в ресторане.
examples.trans: Today the chef is having a very inappropriate day at the restaurant.

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('reasonable, adequate').

examples.trans: I am completely in my right mind!
Chef, you are not in your right mind!

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('necessary, needed').

examples.trans: I need a job too.
Do you need a pen?
He needs money.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'go, walk', paired with 'пойти'.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

examples.text: Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: That's why I'm running for a second term.

examples.text: А ты иди на биржу труда. Там есть работа.
examples.trans: You go to the job centre. There's work there.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'on, onto; for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'видание'). Verbal action/result neuter noun formed with '-ение'/'-ание'. Common neuter noun meaning 'meeting; date' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Goodbye!
I have a date today.
She has a date.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'пытка'). Common feminine noun meaning 'attempt' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Is this an attempt to stop me?

examples.text: На кухне ресторана всегда есть попытка.
examples.trans: In the restaurant kitchen there is always attempt.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'to you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?
And this is for you. A toy car!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'казать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to show', paired with 'показывать'.

examples.trans: Show me your hands!
Shall we show this to Anikeev?

examples.text: Ну, покажите руки. Что у вас за спиной?
examples.trans: Well, show me your hands. What is behind your back?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'host, army (idiomatic)' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I am going to kill Senya, damn it!

examples.text: Этого урода с моей кухни убрать.
examples.trans: Get this freak out of my kitchen.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to want', paired with 'захотеть'.

examples.trans: I want coffee.
If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'бивать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to kill, to murder', paired with 'убить'.

examples.trans: Please, help! They're killing me!
Don't waste time for nothing.
Neighbours! Please, help! They're killing me!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What's this?
Look what I've got.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you.
And where's the toy car?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (stem 'онок'). Formed with a diminutive/expressive Slavic suffix adding warmth or small scale. Common masculine noun meaning 'scumbag, bastard' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Шеф кричал, что вокруг одни подонки.
examples.trans: The chef shouted that there were only scumbags around.

examples.text: Все эти люди вокруг — неблагодарные подонки.
examples.trans: All these people around are ungrateful scumbags.
